metadata.headline: Jane Goodall, Who Chronicled the Social Lives of Chimps, Dies at 91
metadata.speaker: am

sentences.sentence: Jane Goodall, one of the world’s most revered conservationists, who earned scientific stature and global celebrity by chronicling the distinctive behavior of wild chimpanzees in East Africa — primates that made and used tools, ate meat, held rain dances and engaged in organized warfare — died on Wednesday in Los Angeles.
She was 91.
Her death, while on a speaking tour, was confirmed by the Jane Goodall Institute, whose U.S. headquarters are in Washington, D.C.
When not traveling widely, she lived in Bournemouth, on the south coast of England, in her childhood home.
Dr.

Goodall was 29 in the summer of 1963 when National Geographic magazine published her 7,500-word, 37-page account of the lives of primates she had observed in the Gombe Stream Chimpanzee Reserve in what is now Tanzania.
The National Geographic Society had been financially supporting her field studies there.
The article, with photographs by Hugo van Lawick, a Dutch wildlife photographer whom she later married, also described Dr.
Goodall’s struggles to overcome disease, predators and frustration as she tried to get close to the chimps, working from a primitive research station along the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika.

On the scientific merits alone, her discoveries about how wild chimpanzees raised their young, established leadership, socialized and communicated broke new ground and attracted immense attention and respect among researchers.
Stephen Jay Gould, the evolutionary biologist and science historian, said her work with chimpanzees “represents one of the Western world’s great scientific achievements.”
I attribute learning about Jane Goodall as a child to why I chose to go into environmental science.
Women in science will always be important.
It is beyond important for all of us to continue the work.
Rest in peace 🤍
Her insistence on the individuality and personhood of chimpanzees was absolutely groundbreaking.
She should also be honored as a great writer and conservationist.
At a time when writing for so-called popular audiences was looked down upon by the scientific establishment, she produced beautifully written accounts of her work for a general audience.
The last decades of her life were spent in tireless advocacy for animal rights and conservation, with a strong focus on spreading the message of hope to young people.

I am devastated, she was such a close and good friend over the years we spent in Africa and we shared many experiences in establishing chimp sanctuaries in The Congo and other countries in West Africa.
She was one of a kind, and will be missed greatly, RIP dear friend.
She was my childhood hero, and when I met her in person the first time at UW's Kane Hall, her pant-hoot greeting moved me deeply.
She signed her book and told me that teachers we her heroes.
I met her again when I had the chance to drive her around in my car for the Bumbershoot festival, this time, as an educator.
She's the reason I keep teaching middle school science students--like Jane 6th graders are untrained, wildly observant (as humans are), and like Jane says, they are the hope for the future.
I was lucky to follow in her footsteps--In Gombe and in as a scholar practitioner in the work of science education.
The number of former students reaching out to me today is a testament of her reach.
May her memory remain a blessing.
What a remarkable mind and what a remarkable life.
Dr.
Goodall opened a window onto the world of our closest primate relatives and showed us that we humans aren't so different and apart from the natural world.
Rest in peace.
May we be as good stewards of life on this planet as she hoped we'd be.
